bib.title: Harnessing the Power of LLMs in Practice: A Survey on ChatGPT and Beyond

question: When should a practitioner use an LLM rather than a fine-tuned smaller model for a downstream NLP task, given the model, data and task?
contributions: A practitioner guide to GPT-style and BERT-style LLMs
Discussion of how pre-training, fine-tuning and test data affect model choice
Use and non-use cases for LLMs across NLU, generation, knowledge-intensive, scaling/emergent and real-world tasks, summarised as a decision flow (Fig 2)
Discussion of efficiency, cost, latency, PEFT, trustworthiness and safety

results.claim: The authors define fine-tuned models as typically smaller than 20B parameters, as a practical cut-off.
results.setup: Authors' working definition; not an experiment
results.quote: From a practical standpoint, we consider models with less than 20B parameters to be fine-tuned models.

results.claim: On CivilComments toxicity detection even the best LLM only beats random guessing, while popular fine-tuned models do much better.
results.setup: HELM evaluation of prompted LLMs, quoted by the survey
results.quote: on CivilComments [13] even the best one is only better than random guessing [59]

results.claim: Perspective API, a fine-tuned multilingual BERT-based model with distilled single-language CNNs, remains among the best toxicity detectors.
results.quote: This API is powered by a multilingual BERT-based model, which is tuned on publicly available toxicity data and several smaller single-language CNNs distilled from this model.

results.claim: On CoNLL03 NER, fine-tuned models perform around twice as well as LLMs.
results.setup: CoNLL03 NER; LLMs evaluated per Ohashi/Ruder-style cited work [81]
results.quote: where the performance of fine-tuned models is around as twice as LLMs

results.claim: LLMs are usually 10x or even 100x larger than fine-tuned models.
results.quote: The scale of LLMs is usually 10× or even 100× larger than fine-tuned models.

results.claim: GPT-4 reaches 86.5% accuracy on English MMLU.
results.quote: outperforms existing models by a considerable margin in English with a satisfactory 86.5% accuracy
GPT-4 has been close to the performance of 100% (96.3%) [76]

results.claim: Training the 11B T5 costs well over $1.3 million per run and one GPT-3 175B run costs $4.6 million.
results.setup: Estimates from a Lambda Labs blog post
results.quote: training the 11B parameter variant of T5 costs well over $1.3 million for a single run, while a single training run of GPT-3 175B requires $4.6 million [3]

results.claim: GPT-3 175B needs 3.14 x 10^23 FLOPs, ten times a T5 11B.
results.quote: GPT-3 175B requiring 3.14 × 1023 Flops, while a T5 11B model only requires 3.30 × 1022

results.claim: OpenAI custom-model fine-tuning cost $0.03 per 1k training tokens and $0.12 per 1k usage tokens, versus $0.002 per 1k for GPT-3.5-turbo chat (March 2023 pricing).
results.unit: USD per 1k tokens (usage of custom model)
results.setup: OpenAI pricing page accessed 03/02/2023; has dated
results.quote: training costs $0.03 per 1k tokens, while usage costs $0.12 per 1k tokens [4]

results.claim: GPT-J 6B inference time grows from 0.077s at max 2 tokens to 0.707s at 32 tokens; InstructGPT davinci v2 takes 1.969s at 32 tokens.
results.quote: the inference time for the GPT-J 6B model is 0.077s, 0.203s, and 0.707s when the max token size is set to 2, 8, and 32

results.claim: InstructGPT davinci v2 (175B*) scoring a query-passage pair takes 0.21s, too slow for web search.
results.quote: 0.21s per request (i.e., a query-passage pair to be scored), which is too slow for web search engines

results.claim: Alpaca-LoRA runs LLaMA-Alpaca tuning within hours on a single RTX 4090.
results.setup: LoRA on LLaMA, per the Alpaca-LoRA GitHub repo
results.quote: enables runs LLaMA within hours on a single RTX 4090

results.claim: Fine-tuning on application data can worsen zero-shot robustness and calibration.
results.quote: the robustness of the zero-shot becomes worse after being tuned on extra application-specific tasks data [116]

results.claim: Recommendation: choose light, local fine-tuned models over LLMs when cost or latency matters, and use parameter-efficient tuning for deployment.
results.quote: Light, local, fine-tuned models should be considered rather than LLMs, especially for those who are sensitive to the cost or have strict latency requirements.

limits: Survey: no experiments of its own; every performance claim is quoted from other work, often via HELM or PaLM.
PEFT gets one paragraph (LoRA, prefix tuning, P-tuning, Alpaca-LoRA) with no numbers or hyperparameters.
Authors concede there is no systematic comparison of fine-tuned models and LLMs on real-world tasks.
Pricing, model landscape and the 'under 20B is fine-tunable' cut-off date from early 2023.
No QLoRA, DoRA or adapter coverage.
practices: Prefer LLMs for out-of-distribution data and limited annotated data (Remark 1, s3).
Prefer fine-tuned models for traditional NLU tasks with rich annotated data and little OOD (Remark 2, s4.1).
Use LLMs for generation tasks (Remark 3, s4.2), but test generated code carefully (s4.2.1).
Use retrieval augmentation to make closed-book tasks open-book, after which small fine-tuned models do well (s4.3.2).
Consider small fine-tuned models for cost- or latency-sensitive deployment, and parameter-efficient tuning (Remark 8, s5.1).
Pick a model pre-trained on data similar to the downstream task (Remark 1(3), s3.1).

terms.definition: LLMs are huge language models pretrained on large amounts of datasets without tuning on data for specific tasks
fine-tuned models are typically smaller language models which are also pretrained and then further tuned on a smaller, task-specific dataset to optimize their performance on that task
an efficient technique to tune a small portation of model parameters (or extra parameters) while freezing most parameters of the pre-trained LLMs
abilities that are not present in smaller-scale models but are present in large-scale models
